title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
tagline: Dive deep before backtracking — the basis of connectivity, cycles, and topological order.

intuition.analogy: Exploring a cave with a ball of string: you follow one passage as far as it goes, and only when you hit a dead end do you backtrack along the string to the last junction and try another passage.
paragraphs: DFS explores as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking. Implemented with recursion (or an explicit stack), it naturally enumerates connected components and detects structure within a graph.
Its real power is in what it reveals through timing: discovery/finish times expose cycles, topological order (post-order reversed), bridges, articulation points, and strongly connected components.
Like BFS it runs in O(V+E), but it does NOT find shortest paths in general — its strength is structural analysis, not distance.
intuition.keyIdea: Recurse into unvisited neighbours, backtracking at dead ends; visit order and finish order encode graph structure.

steps.title: Visit and mark
steps.detail: On entering a node, mark it visited so you never re-enter it.

steps.title: Recurse into neighbours
steps.detail: For each unvisited neighbour, recurse. This dives deep before exploring siblings.

steps.title: Backtrack
steps.detail: When all neighbours are explored, return to the caller. Post-order (finish) time is recorded here — useful for topo sort and SCC.

complexity.timeReason: Each vertex is entered once; each edge is examined once.
complexity.spaceReason: Recursion stack and visited set, up to V deep/large.

pitfalls: Recursion depth can overflow on large/deep graphs — use an explicit stack if needed.
DFS does not yield shortest paths.
For directed-cycle detection, track three colours (white/gray/black), not just a binary visited flag.

dryRun.clickMoment: DFS commits fully to one branch (0→1→3) before ever touching node 2. The recursion stack IS the current root-to-node path — which is exactly why backtracking algorithms are DFS in disguise.
